questions.q: Why can't ShopFlow wrap "charge, reserve, book courier" in one BEGIN … COMMIT any more?
questions.explain: A transaction is a promise made by one database. With four databases (and a payment provider's HTTP API), no single system can promise all-or-nothing across them.
options: PostgreSQL does not allow more than one statement per transaction
Each service owns its own database, and a transaction only covers one database connection
Transactions are too slow for checkout
The payment provider forbids transactions

questions.q: In two-phase commit, what does a participant promise when it votes "yes" in the prepare phase?
questions.explain: After voting yes, the participant can no longer decide on its own. That is what makes 2PC atomic, and what makes a coordinator failure so painful.
options: That it has already committed
That it has done and durably saved the work, keeps its locks, and will commit if told to, even after a crash
That it will retry the work later
That the other participants will also vote yes

questions.q: The coordinator crashes after every participant voted yes but before it sent "commit". What happens?
questions.explain: A prepared participant cannot know whether the others were told to commit or abort, so neither choice is safe. Rows stay locked and other customers wait.
options: The participants commit after a timeout
The participants roll back after a timeout
The participants stay in doubt, holding their locks, until the coordinator returns or an operator resolves the transaction
The fastest participant becomes the new coordinator automatically

questions.q: Four services are each available 99.9% of the time. Roughly how often are all four available together, as a 2PC transaction needs?
questions.explain: 0.999⁴ ≈ 0.996. A protocol that needs every participant at once multiplies their unavailability: about 35 hours a year instead of 9.
options: About 99.6%
About 96%
100%, because failures cancel out

questions.q: Why can't a payment provider's REST API take part in 2PC with ShopFlow's databases?
questions.explain: A participant must implement prepare, commit and abort. HTTP APIs, message brokers and e-mail services generally do not, which is one of the main reasons sagas exist.
options: REST APIs are too slow
It offers no prepare phase: it cannot hold a charge "prepared but not committed" under ShopFlow's control
2PC only works with MySQL
Payment providers use a different time zone

questions.q: What is a saga?
questions.explain: Each step commits immediately in one service's database. Consistency comes from compensations, not from rollback.
options: A long database transaction held open across services
A sequence of local transactions, each committed on its own, with compensations that undo finished steps if a later one fails
A log of every event in the system
A retry policy with backoff

questions.q: The saga must undo a captured ₦25,000 payment. Which compensation is right?
questions.explain: A compensation is a new business action that semantically undoes the old one. The charge happened, the customer's bank shows it, and the refund is another fact next to it.
options: Delete the payment row
Roll back the payments database to its state before the charge
Refund the payment: a new, visible record in the payments ledger
Nothing: money cannot be returned

questions.q: Steps "charge", "reserve" and "book courier" succeeded; "confirm order" then fails permanently. In which order do the compensations run?
questions.explain: Compensations run in reverse order, like unwinding a stack, so each one finds the world as its step left it.
options: Refund, release, cancel courier
Cancel courier, release, refund
All at once, in parallel
Only the refund, since money matters most

questions.q: A saga step sends the customer a "your order is confirmed" SMS. Later, a step fails. What is the compensation?
questions.explain: Some steps cannot be undone. Put them last, after the steps that can fail, or accept a compensating message instead of an undo.
options: Delete the SMS
There is none that removes it; the best you can do is send a correction ("your order was cancelled, you have been refunded")
Retry the SMS
Roll back the SMS provider

questions.q: What is the pivot of a saga?
questions.explain: Before the pivot, failures compensate. After it, failures are retried until the saga completes. Irreversible steps belong at or after the pivot.
options: The first step
The step after which the saga can no longer compensate, so it must go forward to completion
The orchestrator process
The step with the most retries

questions.q: 20% of orders fail because the item is out of stock. Why is "reserve, then charge" better than "charge, then reserve"?
questions.explain: Put steps that fail often and are cheap to undo first, and expensive or irreversible ones last. The practice section measured 18 refunds against 0.
options: Reserving is faster than charging
Out-of-stock orders then fail before any money moves, so they need no refund; only the rare declined card needs a cheap stock release
Charging first is not allowed by payment providers
It makes the saga isolated

questions.q: While a checkout saga runs, another request reads the order. What should it see, and how is that handled?
questions.explain: Sagas have no isolation: each step is committed and visible. Design for it: explicit pending states, and code that treats them as "in progress, do not touch".
options: Nothing: sagas are isolated like database transactions
An intermediate state such as pending; the status acts as a semantic lock that tells other code the order is in progress
The final state, because sagas complete instantly
An error until the saga finishes

questions.q: The charge step times out. The saga does not know whether the card was charged. What should it do?
questions.explain: An unknown outcome is resolved by asking again safely. With the same key there is exactly one charge either way. A new key could charge twice.
options: Assume it failed and compensate
Assume it succeeded and continue
Retry the charge with the same idempotency key, so payments returns the existing charge or makes it now
Charge again with a new key to be sure

questions.q: Why must every saga step and compensation be idempotent?
questions.explain: The step's effect and the orchestrator's progress live in different databases and cannot be saved atomically. So "at least once" is the best guarantee, and idempotency turns it into "effectively once".
options: So they can run in parallel
A durable orchestrator can crash after a step's effect but before saving its progress, so on resume the step runs again
Because PostgreSQL requires it
So the saga finishes faster

questions.q: A refund compensation returns 503. What should the orchestrator do?
questions.explain: A saga that stops compensating halfway leaves the customer charged without an order. Compensations have no "give up" branch, so design them so they can always eventually succeed.
options: Give up and mark the saga failed
Skip the refund and cancel the order
Retry it (with backoff) until it succeeds, and alert a human if it keeps failing
Charge the customer again

questions.q: Which statement about orchestration and choreography is right?
questions.explain: An orchestrator can be read top to bottom and answers "where is order 42?" with one row. Choreography suits short reactions where services should not know about each other.
options: Choreography keeps the whole flow in one place
Orchestration keeps the flow and its state in one component, which suits multi-step flows with compensations such as checkout
Orchestration needs no idempotency
Choreography cannot use events

questions.q: What is a real cost of choreography?
questions.explain: No service knows the whole flow. That keeps them decoupled, and also makes the flow hard to see, change and debug, and makes accidental cycles easy.
options: It needs a central database
The flow is spread across services' event handlers, so changing it touches several services and debugging means following events through all of them
It can only have two steps
It forbids compensations

questions.q: A service saves an order, then publishes order.placed to the broker. What can go wrong?
questions.explain: That is a dual write: two systems, no shared transaction, a crash window in between. Reordering the calls just moves the bug (an event for an order that was never saved).
options: Nothing, if both calls are awaited
The process can crash between the two, leaving a saved order whose event is never sent
The event arrives before the order is saved
The broker rejects events for saved orders

questions.q: What makes the transactional outbox reliable?
questions.explain: "Send a message" becomes "insert a row", which the database's transaction protects. The relay retries publishing until the row is marked published.
options: It publishes events faster
The event is written as a row in the same local transaction as the business change, so both are saved or neither is; a relay publishes it afterwards
It uses two-phase commit with the broker
It deletes events after one delivery attempt

questions.q: The relay publishes an outbox row, then crashes before marking it published. What happens next?
questions.explain: That is why the outbox gives at-least-once delivery. Duplicates are handled on the consumer side, with an inbox or idempotent operations.
options: The event is lost
The next relay run publishes it again, so consumers may receive it twice
The database rolls back the publish
The broker deduplicates it automatically

questions.q: Two relay instances claim outbox rows with … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. What does SKIP LOCKED do?
questions.explain: Without it, the second relay would wait for the first relay's lock, then publish the same rows. With it, work is shared out. (PGlite is a single connection, so the lesson could show the query but not two relays competing.)
options: It unlocks rows after reading them
A relay skips rows that another relay has locked instead of waiting for them, so they claim different rows
It skips rows that were already published
It makes the query read-only

questions.q: Why must the inbox insert be in the same transaction as the charge it protects?
questions.explain: Recording "done" and doing it must be atomic. Recorded without the effect, the message is lost; the effect without the record, it is repeated.
options: To make the query faster
If the charge fails and rolls back, the inbox row rolls back too, so a redelivery is processed properly instead of being skipped as "already done"
Because PostgreSQL requires every insert to be in a transaction
So the relay can read it

questions.q: A relay gives each send a fresh random message id. Why does that break the consumer's inbox?
questions.explain: The id must identify the message, not the delivery. Deriving it from the outbox row (or the event's own id) keeps it the same on every attempt.
options: Random ids are too long for the table
A redelivery of the same outbox row arrives with a different id, so the inbox cannot recognise it as a duplicate
Random ids are not unique
It does not break anything

questions.q: Why does the orchestrator save the saga's step and status in the orders database after every step?
questions.explain: An orchestrator that keeps progress only in memory forgets every saga in flight when it dies: money charged, no order, and nobody knows.
options: For reporting only
So a new process can resume an interrupted saga after a crash, continuing forward or compensating from where it stopped
Because the steps need a transaction
To make the saga isolated

questions.q: The orders service starts the saga in a @zudojs/transactions after-commit callback. If the saga throws there, what happens?
questions.explain: After-commit work cannot undo the commit. That is why the saga row is written in the transaction: the database, not the callback, is the source of truth.
options: The order's transaction is rolled back
The error is thrown to placeOrder's caller
The data is already committed, so the manager reports the error to hooks.onError instead; resume() on startup or a timer must pick the saga up
The saga is retried automatically by the manager

questions.q: The lesson's relay claims rows by setting claimed_until to a short time in the future. Why a lease instead of a permanent "claimed" flag?
questions.explain: Any claim made by a process that can die needs an expiry. The same idea protects sagas from two orchestrators working on them at once.
options: Leases use less disk space
If the relay crashes after claiming, the lease runs out and another relay picks the rows up; a permanent flag would strand them
Leases make delivery exactly once
PostgreSQL cannot store booleans

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Needing four systems up at once multiplies their availability: 0.999⁴ ≈ 0.996, about four times the downtime of one.
options: 99.60% 35 hours a year
99.90% 9 hours a year
99.60% 9 hours a year
96.00% 350 hours a year

questions.explain: Only completed steps are undone, newest first. The failed step committed nothing, and "ship" never ran.
options:
undo charge
undo order
cancelled

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The redelivered m1 is recognised by its id. The check and the record happen with no await in between, which is what makes this safe in one process; in a database, a unique key plays that role.
options: m1: stock 8 | m2: stock 7 | m1: skipped
m1: stock 8 | m2: stock 7 | m1: stock 5
m1: stock 8 | m2: skipped | m1: skipped
m1: skipped | m2: stock 9 | m1: stock 7

questions.q: Two deliveries of the same message arrive at once. What does this print?
questions.explain: Both m1 deliveries passed the check before either recorded it, so m1 was charged twice. The set still has two entries, because adding the same id twice changes nothing. Check-then-act across an await is a race.

questions.q: A compensation runs twice after a crash. What does this print?
questions.explain: The release only acts on a reservation that is still reserved, so the second run is a no-op and stock goes up once. That is what "idempotent compensation" looks like in code.
options: released nothing to do 5
released released 6
released nothing to do 4
nothing to do nothing to do 4

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first attempt charged the card and lost the answer. The retry used the same key, found the charge and returned it. One charge, and the saga knows it succeeded.
options:
attempt 1: timeout
attempt 2: captured
charges: 1

attempt 1: timeout
attempt 2: captured
charges: 2

attempt 1: captured
charges: 1

attempt 1: timeout
attempt 2: timeout
attempt 3: captured
charges: 1

questions.q: An orchestrator saved { step: 2, status: "compensating" } before crashing. What does the new one print when it resumes?
questions.explain: step counts completed steps. Compensating from step 2 undoes steps 1 and 0 (reserve, charge); running from step 1 continues with reserve and ship. A completed saga needs nothing.
options:
undo reserve, undo charge
run reserve, run ship
nothing to do

undo ship, undo reserve, undo charge
run reserve, run ship
nothing to do

undo charge, undo reserve
run charge, run reserve, run ship
nothing to do

undo reserve, undo charge
run reserve, run ship
run ship

questions.q: An in-memory outbox and relay. What does this print?
questions.explain: The relay delivered row 1 and crashed before marking it, so the next run delivered it again, then row 2. The third run found nothing. At-least-once: every row arrives, row 1 twice.

questions.q: A small choreography on @zudojs/events. What does this print?
questions.explain: Each service reacts to the previous event. The compensation (releasing stock) is just another reaction, which is why the full flow is only visible by following the chain.
options: order.placed -> stock.reserved -> payment.declined -> stock.released -> order.cancelled
order.placed -> stock.reserved -> payment.declined -> order.cancelled
order.placed -> payment.declined -> stock.released -> order.cancelled
order.placed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A cancelled order with a captured payment is the ₦25,000 bug. A pending order at the end of a test means a saga was left unfinished, which the invariant must also treat as a failure.
options: true true false false
true true true false
true false false false
true true false true

questions.q: Write runSaga(steps). Each step has name, run() and undo(). Run the steps in order, logging done NAME. If one throws, log failed NAME: MESSAGE, run the undo of every completed step in reverse order logging undone NAME, and return "cancelled". Otherwise return "confirmed".
questions.explain: Compensations run newest first. Copying before reversing ([...done].reverse()) avoids changing the list in place, a habit that matters when the list is also saved as the saga's progress.
questions.expected:
done charge
done reserve
failed ship: no courier available
undone reserve
undone charge
cancelled
done charge
done reserve
confirmed

questions.q: Fix consume so that two simultaneous deliveries of the same message charge once. Claim the id before the await, and if the charge fails, remove the claim so a later redelivery can try again.
questions.explain: Claiming first closes the race; releasing the claim on failure plays the role of the rollback that removes the inbox row when the charge fails. In a database both come for free from putting the inbox insert and the charge in one transaction.

questions.q: Write an idempotent charge(key, orderId, amountKobo) for the payments service. The first call with a key stores { orderId, amountKobo, status: "captured" } and returns "charged"; later calls with the same key return "already charged" without storing anything. Also write refund(key) that changes a captured payment to "refunded" and returns "refunded", or "nothing to refund".
questions.explain: Both operations are safe to repeat: the key stops a second charge, and the status check stops a second refund. Refunding an unknown key is also safe, which matters when a compensation runs for a step whose effect never happened.
questions.expected:
charged
already charged
refunded nothing to refund nothing to refund
1 refunded

questions.q: Write relay(outbox, publish): for every row with published: false, in id order, call publish(row) and then set published = true. If publish throws, stop and leave that row (and later ones) unpublished. Return how many rows were published.
questions.explain: Publishing in id order keeps events in the order they were written, and stopping at the first failure preserves that order when the broker comes back. The row stays in the outbox until it is really out.
questions.expected:
published 1 order.placed
published 2 payment.captured
run 1: 2
published 3 stock.reserved
run 2: 1
run 3: 0

questions.q: Write resume(saga, steps) for a saga stored as { step, status }, where step is the number of completed steps. If running, run the remaining steps (log run NAME) and set status completed. If compensating, undo completed steps newest first (log undo NAME) and set status cancelled. Update saga.step after each step so a crash could resume again.
questions.explain: The same counter serves both directions: forward it counts completed steps, backward it counts steps still to undo. Saving it after every step is what makes the orchestrator restartable at any point.
questions.expected:
run reserve
run ship
undo reserve
undo charge
{ step: 3, status: 'completed' } { step: 0, status: 'cancelled' }

questions.q: Write an idempotent reserve(key, sku, quantity): if the key was already reserved, return "already reserved"; if there is not enough stock, throw new Error(SKU + " is out of stock"); otherwise reduce stock, remember the key and return "reserved, N left".
questions.explain: The repeated key after a crash does not take a second lamp. In PostgreSQL the same logic is one transaction: check the reservation, UPDATE … WHERE available >= $2, insert the reservation.
questions.expected:
reserved, 1 left
already reserved
reserved, 0 left
lamp is out of stock

questions.q: Build a tiny choreography with a Map of handlers. When order.placed arrives, payments emits payment.captured; inventory then emits stock.reserved if stock > 0 (and decrements it) or stock.rejected; on stock.rejected, payments emits payment.refunded. Print each event as it is emitted. Place two orders with 1 lamp in stock.
questions.explain: The refund is a reaction to stock.rejected, registered by payments. Nobody holds the whole flow: to know why ord_2 was refunded you follow the chain of events, which is exactly the trade-off of choreography.
questions.expected:
ord_1: order.placed
ord_1: payment.captured
ord_1: stock.reserved
ord_2: order.placed
ord_2: payment.captured
ord_2: stock.rejected
ord_2: payment.refunded

questions.q: Write check(runs) for a crash test. Each run is { crashAt, order, payment, shipment, lampsBefore, lampsAfter }. A run is consistent when it is confirmed (payment captured, shipment booked, one lamp fewer) or cancelled (payment not captured, shipment not booked, lamps unchanged). Print INCONSISTENT crash CRASHAT for each bad run, then N of M consistent.
questions.explain: "After reserve" took two lamps: the reservation was not idempotent and ran twice on resume. "After undo charge" left a captured payment on a cancelled order: the refund was lost. Each inconsistency points straight at the step that needs fixing.
questions.expected:
INCONSISTENT crash after reserve
INCONSISTENT crash after undo charge
2 of 4 consistent
